Learning Objectives (2026)
1. Recognize the characteristic neurological signs and symptoms associated
with lesions involving brainstem nuclei, cranial nerve fascicles, long tracts,
and vascular territories. (CLO 3)
2. Apply knowledge of brainstem anatomy and associated neurological deficits
to localize common brainstem syndromes. (CLO 3)
Pre-Class Assignment:
• Preview the PowerPoint slides. You are not expected to memorize details before class.
• Review the major brainstem and cranial nerve concepts from Session 3 – Brainstem and
Cranial Nerves I, with particular attention to cranial nerve nuclei, long tracts, and vascular
territories.
• Watch: Rule of 4s (15 min)

Blood Supply – Circle of Willis
Anterior Circulation
• Internal carotid artery → ACA, MCA
Posterior Circulation
• Vertebral arteries → PICA
• Vertebral arteries unite → Basilar artery
• Basilar artery branches → AICA, SCA, pontine aa.
• Basilar artery terminates as → PCA
Communicating Arteries
• Anterior communicating artery (ACOM)
• Posterior communicating arteries (PCOM)
Fig. 7.2 The arrangement of arterial vessels on the base of the brain. The
diagram shows the circulus arteriosus (circle of Willis).
Crossman, Neuroanatomy: An Illustrated Color Text, 6e.

Major Arterial Supply
Midbrain
• Posterior cerebral artery (PCA)
• Superior cerebellar artery (SCA)
Pons
• Pontine branches of basilar artery
• Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA)
• Superior cerebellar artery (SCA)
Medulla
• Vertebral artery
• Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)
• Anterior spinal artery
Fig. 7.2 The arrangement of arterial vessels on the base of the brain. The
diagram shows the circulus arteriosus (circle of Willis).
Crossman, Neuroanatomy: An Illustrated Color Text, 6e.

Brainstem Localization: A Four-Step Approach
1. Cranial nerve deficit → LEVEL
• Midbrain → III, IV
• Pons → V–VIII
• Medulla → IX, X, XII
2. Body deficit → LONG TRACT
• Weakness → corticospinal
• Vibration/proprioception → medial lemniscus
• Pain/temperature → spinothalamic
3. Determine LOCATION
• Medial vs lateral
4. Identify VASCULAR TERRITORY
• Match the involved structures to the artery
CN → Level | Body → Tract | Medial/Lateral → Location | Artery → Syndrome

The Crossed Brainstem Pattern
Brainstem Lesions: Face vs Body
• Cranial nerve nuclei/fascicles affect the ipsilateral head/face
• Long tracts may produce contralateral body deficits
• Therefore, brainstem lesions commonly produce crossed neurological findings
Example
• Ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss
• Contralateral body pain/temperature loss
→ Brainstem lesion
Brainstem Lesion
Ipsilateral cranial nerve/face deficit + contralateral body deficit → think BRAINSTEM
Berkowitz. Clinical Neurology and Neuroanatomy. McGraw Hill.

Medial vs Lateral Localization
Medial
• Corticospinal tract → motor
• Medial lemniscus → vibration/proprioception
• MLF → conjugate eye movements
• Medially located motor CN nuclei/fascicles
Lateral
• Spinothalamic tract → body pain/temperature
• Spinal trigeminal system → facial pain/temperature
• Cerebellar pathways → coordination
• Descending sympathetic fibers → sympathetic function
• Selected sensory/autonomic CN nuclei
Central Medulla
Medial → motor + medial lemniscus | Lateral → pain/temp + cerebellar/autonomic
Fig. 9.8. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Horner Syndrome
Cause: Interruption of sympathetic innervation to the head
Classic Findings
• Miosis → loss of pupillary dilator
• Mild ptosis → loss of superior tarsal muscle
• Anhidrosis → loss of sympathetic innervation to sweat glands
Brainstem Localization
• Descending hypothalamospinal sympathetic fibers travel
through the lateral brainstem
• Lateral brainstem lesion → ipsilateral Horner syndrome
Ptosis: CN III Palsy Partial Ptosis: loss of superior tarsal innervation
Fig. 8.74 Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 3e.
Image: American Academy of Ophthalmology website
Image: Wikipedia

Medial Medulla: Localize the Structures
Identify three structures:
• Pyramid / corticospinal tract → body motor
• Medial lemniscus → vibration/proprioception
• CN XII fascicle → tongue motor
Central Medulla
If these three structures were injured together, what would you predict?
Fig. 9.8. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Medial Medullary Syndrome (Dejerine Syndrome)
Structure Deficit
Corticospinal tract Contralateral body weakness
Medial lemniscus Contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception
Ipsilateral tongue weakness → deviation
CN XII fascicle
toward lesion
Vascular territory: anterior spinal or vertebral artery branches
Ipsilateral XII deficit + contralateral motor/proprioception loss
→ medial medulla
Waxman, 28e.

Lateral Medulla: Localize the Structures
Focus only on:
• Nucleus ambiguus
• Spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract
• Spinothalamic tract
• Inferior cerebellar peduncle
• Vestibular nuclei
• Descending sympathetic fibers
Central Medulla
Swallowing/voice + crossed pain/temp + ataxia/autonomic findings → lateral medulla
Fig. 9.8. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome
Structure Deficit
Nucleus ambiguus Dysphagia, hoarseness
Spinal trigeminal system Ipsilateral facial pain/temp loss
Spinothalamic tract Contralateral body pain/temp loss
Inferior cerebellar peduncle Ipsilateral ataxia
Vestibular nuclei Vertigo, nystagmus
Descending sympathetics Ipsilateral Horner syndrome
Vascular territory: PICA or vertebral artery
Nucleus ambiguus
involvement is the key clue to lateral medulla
Waxman, 28e.

Medial Pons: Localize the Structures
Identify three structures:
• Corticospinal tract → body motor
• Medial lemniscus → vibration/proprioception
• CN VI fascicle → lateral rectus motor
Caudal Pons
If these three structures were injured together, what would you predict?
Fig. 10.5. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Medial Pontine Syndrome
Structure Deficit
Corticospinal tract Contralateral body weakness
Medial lemniscus Contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception
CN VI fascicle Ipsilateral impaired eye abduction
Vascular territory: paramedian branches of the basilar artery
Caudal Pons
Ipsilateral CN VI + contralateral motor/proprioception → medial pons
Fig. 10.5. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Lateral Pons – Localize the Structures
Key structures
• Facial nucleus/fascicle (CN VII)
• Vestibular/cochlear structures (CN VIII)
• Spinal trigeminal system
• Spinothalamic tract
• Cerebellar connections
• Descending sympathetic fibers
Caudal Pons
CN VII/VIII findings → think PONS
Fig. 10.4. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Lateral Pontine Syndrome
Structure Deficit
Facial nucleus/fascicle (CN VII) Ipsilateral facial paralysis
Vestibular nuclei (CN VIII) Vertigo, nystagmus
Cochlear nuclei/pathway (CN VIII) Ipsilateral hearing loss
Spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract Ipsilateral facial pain/temp loss
Spinothalamic tract Contralateral body pain/temp loss
Middle/inferior cerebellar peduncle Ipsilateral ataxia
Caudal Pons
Descending sympathetic fibers Ipsilateral Horner syndrome
Vascular territory: AICA
Facial paralysis → AICA/pons | Dysphagia + hoarseness → PICA/medulla
Fig. 10.5. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Lateral Pons vs Lateral Medulla
AICA — Pons PICA — Medulla
Level clue CN VII/VIII CN IX/X
Facial paralysis Yes No
Dysphagia/hoarseness No/less characteristic Yes
Ipsilateral face pain/temp ↓ Yes Yes
Contralateral body pain/temp ↓ Yes Yes
Ataxia/vertigo Yes Yes
Facial weakness → AICA | Hoarseness/dysphagia → PICA

Medial Midbrain Localization
Key structures
• CN III fascicles
• Cerebral peduncle / corticospinal tract
Predict the findings:
• CN III → ipsilateral oculomotor palsy
• Corticospinal → contralateral body weakness
CN III + contralateral weakness → medial midbrain
Midbrain – superior colliculus level
Fig. 11.5. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Weber Syndrome
Structure Deficit
CN III fascicle Ipsilateral CN III palsy
Corticospinal tract Contralateral body weakness
Corticobulbar tract Contralateral lower facial weakness
Location: ventromedial midbrain
Vascular territory: PCA branches
Midbrain – superior colliculus level, Waxman, 28e.
Ipsilateral CN III + contralateral motor deficits → medial midbrain

Dorsal Midbrain (Parinaud) Syndrome
• Location: dorsal midbrain / pretectal region
• Impaired upward gaze (vertical gaze palsy)
• Pupils constrict to near, but not to light (light-near dissociation)
• Convergence-retraction nystagmus
• Often associated with compression by a pineal region mass
Vertical gaze abnormality → dorsal midbrain
Midbrain – superior colliculus level, Waxman, 28e.

Brainstem Localization
1. Find the cranial nerve deficit → LEVEL
2. Find the body deficit → LONG TRACT
3. Combine the structures → MEDIAL vs LATERAL
4. Identify the vascular territory → ARTERY
5. Only then → NAME THE SYNDROME
Don't memorize syndromes as lists; localize the anatomy
